claims.text: Controlled thermomechanical processing can produce a high and uniformly distributed density of deformation twins in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
A high, uniformly distributed twin density will improve ductility under dynamic impact loading.
A high, uniformly distributed twin density will improve uniform deformability under dynamic impact loading.
Twin-promoting thermomechanical processing will preserve the alloy's high strength while improving ductility.
Twin-promoting thermomechanical processing will preserve impact-induced energy release.
An untreated Ti40Zr40W10Mo10-type refractory alloy has limited ductility and a propensity for localized deformation despite high strength.
The untreated refractory alloy has good energetic performance.
Hot rolling followed by rapid annealing can create a fine microstructure containing a high density of uniformly distributed nanoscale twins in the primary phase.
Mechanical twinning can be an important plastic-deformation mechanism in a high-entropy alloy under high-strain-rate loading.
Finely dispersed twins act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Multiple operative twinning systems can promote substantial uniform plastic deformation.
Induced twins provide additional operative slip systems through twinning-induced plasticity.
Twins interrupt dislocation glide and thereby impede shear localization.
The twin-mediated mechanism will not reduce the material's capacity for rapid energy release during impact.
The untreated baseline has a low twin density and exhibits more localized deformation than the treated material.
The proposed improvement may be specific to impact or high-strain-rate loading and may not extend to quasi-static loading because different deformation mechanisms may dominate.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant ductility and deformation-uniformity improvement while retaining comparable strength and energy release would falsify the hypothesis.
